1.0.0.en: 1 In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah came Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon unto Jerusalem, and besieged it. 2 And the Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, with part of the vessels of the house of God: which he carried into the land of Shinar to the house of his god; and he brought the vessels into the treasure house of his god. 3 And the king spake unto Ashpenaz the master of his eunuchs, that he should bring certain of the children of Israel, and of the king’s seed, and of the princes; 4 Children in whom was no blemish, but well favoured, and skilful in all wisdom, and cunning in knowledge, and understanding science, and such as had ability in them to stand in the king’s palace, and whom they might teach the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans.

1.0.1.en: The book opens with an allusion to the first captivity of Judah in the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim, that is, about 605 B.C., at the hands of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, when he besieged Jerusalem and humbled its king (2 Kgs 24:1; Jer 22:19). He took some of the vessels of the house of the Lord and brought them to Shinar to put them in the treasure house of his god.

1.0.2.en: “In the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah came Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon unto Jerusalem, and besieged it” [1].

1.0.3.en: It is stated here that the captivity took place in the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim (Dan 1:1), whereas in (Jer 25:1) it is the fourth year of his reign. This is because the Assyrians and Babylonians reckoned the year from the new year after the king’s accession to the throne, while in Judah they reckoned it from the beginning of the year in which he ascended the throne; therefore the Assyrian and Babylonian reckoning comes out one year more than the Jewish.

1.0.4.en: Some see that the verb “came” in (Dan 1:1) in Hebrew can mean the beginning of Nebuchadnezzar’s going out at the head of the campaign to resist Necho king of Egypt in the battle of Carchemish, whereas what is stated in Jeremiah refers to his arrival at Jerusalem.

1.0.5.en: Nebuchadnezzar or “Nebuchadrezzar”: a Babylonian name meaning “Nebo protects the boundary,” or “O god Nebo, guard the boundary,” or “O Nebo, guard the succession.” As for “Nebo,” its meaning is “announcement” or “proclamation,” and he is the god of knowledge and learning among the Babylonians. The father of Nebuchadnezzar was Nabopolassar, the founder of the new Babylonian state in 625 B.C. and the destroyer of the Assyrian Empire. He sent his son to fight Necho, Pharaoh of Egypt, and he defeated him in 605 B.C. in the battle of Carchemish (2 Kgs 24:7; Jer 46:2). Then he came to Jerusalem and besieged it, and carried away some of its inhabitants, among them Daniel and his companions. When he heard of the death of his father, he returned to Babylon to take over the kingdom. It is to be noted here that the text does not mention Nebuchadnezzar as king of Babylon during his siege of Jerusalem; he is called king of Babylon by way of what took place afterwards. Or it may be because he was a king sharing the rule with his father, and then ruled alone after his father’s death. Berosus holds that when Nabopolassar had advanced in age and was unable to command, he gave the command of the armies to his son Nebuchadnezzar. He ruled as a co-regent with his father for at least two years.

1.0.6.en: The accounts of Nebuchadnezzar are found in the books of Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Jeremiah and Daniel, and his monuments in Babylon and elsewhere agree with what is stated in the Holy Bible.

1.1.0.en: “And the Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand, with part of the vessels of the house of God: which he carried into the land of Shinar to the house of his god; and he brought the vessels into the treasure house of his god” [2].

1.1.1.en: The Babylonian captivity of Judah took place in three stages: 1. The first deportation: in 606 B.C. or 605 B.C., after the battle of Carchemish in which Nebuchadnezzar defeated Pharaoh Necho of Egypt, and then headed for Jerusalem. In it Daniel and his friends were taken captive, and in it Nebuchadnezzar took some of the vessels of the house of the Lord and put them in the temple of Baal in Babylon, and left King Jehoiakim on the throne as his vassal, subject to his authority. 2. The second deportation: about 598 B.C. or 597 B.C., eight years after the captivity of Daniel, in which Ezekiel was taken captive. This captivity took place when the kings of Judah, Jehoiakim and Jehoiachin, rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar, so the king came and took the rest of the vessels of the temple and its treasures and carried away King Jehoiakim and with him 10,000 captives from among the nobles, the men of the army, and the craftsmen and skilled workers, and he left in Judah only the poor of the people (Ezek 1:1-3; 2 Chr 36:10; 2 Kgs 24:8-20). 3. The last deportation in 588 B.C. or 587 B.C., in which the king came for the third time to punish King Zedekiah for his rebellion, “and he burnt the house of the LORD, and the king’s house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, and every great man’s house burnt he with fire” (2 Kgs 25:9). He also killed the sons of Zedekiah, the last king of Judah, and put out the eyes of the king himself and led him to Babylon bound in chains, and so the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple was accomplished and Jewish society was shattered (2 Kgs 25:1-7; Jer 34:1-7).

1.1.2.en: All this took place in fulfillment of prophecy (Jer 25; 2 Chr 36:14-21), as a collective discipline because of the people’s deviation and their insistence on pagan worship with its abominations, their not keeping the sabbatical years, and their resistance to the voice of God through the prophets.

1.1.3.en: The first captivity took place in the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim according to the Babylonian calendar, which ignores the first part of the year, and this was not accomplished because of Nebuchadnezzar’s bravery or his well-devised military plan, nor by good fortune or chance, but by divine permission to discipline His people. This is what the prophet Daniel affirmed.

1.1.4.en: * The fact that the defeat of Jehoiakim is recorded shows that the victory was by the will of God and not because of the power of his enemies.

1.1.5.en: St. Jerome. God delivered not only the king of Judah but also delivered his house and his holy vessels to be carried by a pagan hand into a pagan temple in Shinar. This is not a breaking of God’s promise to Abraham and his seed, nor of what is said in the Psalm: “For the LORD hath chosen Zion; he hath desired it for his habitation. This is my rest for ever: here will I dwell; for I have desired it” (Ps 132:13-14), for He set a condition: “If thy children will keep my covenant and my testimony that I shall teach them” (Ps 132:12).

1.1.6.en: In order to stir us to repentance and to return to Him in obedience to God, He is ready to deliver His temple and His holy vessels into pagan hands, in order to draw us to Himself as being His temple, the living stones, and the holy vessels whose portion is heaven.

1.1.7.en: The land of Shinar: an ancient name for the region of Babylon, where the plain of Dura was, and also the tower which the migrants coming from the east tried to build up to heaven, and since confusion took place this region was called “Babel,” which means “confusion” or “bewilderment.”

1.1.8.en: St. Jerome presents to us a symbolic interpretation of Nebuchadnezzar’s carrying away some of the vessels of God, saying:

1.1.9.en: [We must observe, by the spiritual interpretation anagogen, that it was not possible for the king of Babylon to carry away all the vessels of God and place them in the house of the idol which he himself had built, but he carries away only a part of the vessels from the house of God. We understand these vessels to be the teachings of truth. For if you study all the works of the philosophers you necessarily find in them a share of the vessels of God. You find, for example, in Plato that God is the maker of the world, and in Zeno, the head of the Stoics, that there are inhabitants in the infernal places and that souls are immortal, and that honor is the only good thing. But because the philosophers mix truth with error, and corrupt a good nature with many evils, therefore it is said that they carried away a share of the vessels of the house of God and not all of them in their completeness and perfection.]

1.1.10.en: This thought was presented forcefully by St. Clement of Alexandria, and was taken up by his disciple Origen.

1.2.0.en: “And the king spake unto Ashpenaz the master of his eunuchs, that he should bring certain of the children of Israel, and of the king’s seed, and of the princes; children in whom was no blemish, but well favoured, and skilful in all wisdom, and cunning in knowledge, and understanding science, and such as had ability in them to stand in the king’s palace, and whom they might teach the learning and the tongue of the Chaldeans” [3-4].

1.2.1.en: Some liberal critics claim that the name Ashpenaz does not appear in the ancient records of Babylon, and that this figure is not historical. But afterwards one of the Assyriologists discovered this name on a clay tablet in the ruins of Babylon, and it is now preserved in the British Museum.

1.2.2.en: The king established an institute in his palace under the supervision of Ashpenaz. Perhaps this institute included many departments, among them a department for the sons of the Jewish nobles, to offer them a course of study suited to their culture and language. The establishment of this institute to graduate wise men to assist the king reveals the king’s wisdom, breadth of vision and seriousness. As for his choosing some youths from the seed of the kings of the Jews and their nobles, this was for several reasons, among them his constant sense of being the victorious man, who takes the youths of the kings and nobles not to humiliate and torture them but to serve his palace and manage the affairs of the state. On the other hand, by this he drives these youths, with the talents they have, to submit to him and not to think of revolting against him on behalf of their country. This also gives a measure of psychological comfort to the common Jews, that there is in the palace someone who represents them.

1.2.3.en: These youths were characterized by the following:

1.2.8.en: * Able to impart learning to others.

1.2.9.en: * Able to stand in the palace, that is, to turn wisdom, knowledge and understanding into work that they practice in their daily lives.

1.2.10.en: With all the nobility, bodily health, wisdom, knowledge and experience they had, the king wanted them to enjoy the culture of his country and its language, in order to pull them away from their belonging to their own people and bind them to his country. In wisdom he did not destroy what they had been endowed with nor belittle them, but wanted to turn their energies to the account of his royal palace.

1.2.11.en: By the learning of the Chaldeans is meant learning their language, their literature and all their culture in the wide sense, such as astronomy, mathematics and laws, together with magic and the interpretation of dreams, etc. As Moses was trained in the wisdom of the Egyptians, so Daniel and his companions were trained in the wisdom of the Chaldeans.

1.3.s.en: 2. Their selection for the king’s service:

1.3.0.en: “5 And the king appointed them a daily provision of the king’s meat, and of the wine which he drank: so nourishing them three years, that at the end thereof they might stand before the king. 6 Now among these were of the children of Judah, Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah: 7 Unto whom the prince of the eunuchs gave names: for he gave unto Daniel the name of Belteshazzar; and to Hananiah, of Shadrach; and to Mishael, of Meshach; and to Azariah, of Abednego” [5-7].

1.3.1.en: It is clear that Nebuchadnezzar bore some traits befitting him as a king, for he chose noble youths to be trained in the learning of the Chaldeans at the expense of the royal palace, and even to eat of the king’s delicacies, not only to stand before him, so that he might boast of their beauty and good appearance, but to be his counselors, supporting him in managing the many branches of the affairs of the state, and he did not despise them because they were of foreign nationalities. We can say that in this matter he was ahead of his time by tens of centuries. He was not like King Ahasuerus (mentioned in the book of Esther), who appointed men to choose girls to satisfy his lusts, but he chose youths to serve society.

1.3.2.en: Why did the king appoint them to eat of his delicacies?

1.3.3.en: The king ordered this with some cunning, for while he bears the appearance of a generous king in his dealings with the captives, he brings them into a life of luxury which removes from them the spirit of revolt against him on behalf of their own people. If by force he took them captive from their country, by luxury he wanted to remove their belonging to their country. It is as though he wanted to destroy Judah by violence as well as by kindness, using every means to demolish them. As for fixing the period of training at three years, after which they would stand before the king, the number 3 refers to the resurrection. The Lord Christ by His resurrection offered us the mystery of the number 3, to give us His risen life and raise us from luxury to heaven. And Nebuchadnezzar offered these youths the mystery of the number 3, to raise them not to heaven but to Babylon. Thus they would die to their homeland to live with a new Chaldean mind.

1.3.4.en: The names of the four of the tribe of Judah reminded them of their belonging to God their God, His presence with them, or their being in His presence.

1.3.7.en: · Mishael or Michael means “who is like God,” or he who is likened to God.

1.3.9.en: Here appears the concern of the fathers of these young men for the salvation of their souls by every means, even through their names, that they might realize their bond with the Lord. As it is stated in the book of Proverbs: “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Prov 22:6).

1.3.10.en: The prince of the eunuchs wanted to cut these young men off from every tie with their past, their culture and their religion, so he gave them new names that bound them to the principal Chaldean gods, that is, Bel, the sun god, the goddess of beauty and the earth, and the goddess of fire.

1.3.11.en: A. Daniel was called “Belteshazzar,” which means “the prince of Bel,” Bel’s prince. Bel was the principal god whom the Babylonians worshipped.

1.3.12.en: B. Hananiah was called “Shadrach,” which means “inspired by the sun god.”

1.3.13.en: C. Mishael was called “Meshach,” which means “from Shak.” The Babylonians worshipped the goddess Venus under this title, who is the goddess of beauty and the earth.

1.3.14.en: D. Azariah was called “Abednego”; it means “servant of the shining fire.”

1.3.15.en: It is not strange that the king should change their names as he wanted to change their language and culture; thus Pharaoh also did with Joseph (Gen 41). But neither of them was able to change their hearts or their thoughts about the Lord and His people and His sanctuaries. But the Lord Christ, when He changed the name of Simon to Peter (Mk 3), and the two sons of Zebedee to sons of thunder... renewed their depths to fit the heavenly mission for which He prepared them.

1.3.17.en: A. He was called in Hebrew Daniel, because the Hebrews saw in him God who judges the evil of the pagans.

1.3.18.en: B. He was called in Chaldean Belteshazzar, because the Chaldeans or Babylonians saw in him a surpassing hidden power, so they counted him the prince of the supreme god “Bel.”

1.3.19.en: C. He was called in the language of heaven and the angels: “the man greatly beloved” (Dan 10:11, 19; 9:23).

1.4.s.en: 3. Their refusal of the king’s delicacies:

1.4.0.en: 8 But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king’s meat, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself. 9 Now God had brought Daniel into favour and tender love with the prince of the eunuchs. 10 And the prince of the eunuchs said unto Daniel, I fear my lord the king, who hath appointed your meat and your drink: for why should he see your faces worse liking than the children which are of your sort? then shall ye make me endanger my head to the king. 11 Then said Daniel to the chief of the cupbearers, whom the prince of the eunuchs had set over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, 12 Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink. 13 Then let our countenances be looked upon before thee, and the countenance of the children that eat of the portion of the king’s meat: and as thou seest, deal with thy servants. 14 So he consented to them in this matter, and proved them ten days.

1.4.1.en: “But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king’s meat, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.

1.4.2.en: Now God had brought Daniel into favour and tender love with the prince of the eunuchs” [8-9].

1.4.3.en: Since Daniel was faithful to God, the Lord gave him favor in the eyes of the prince of the eunuchs, and as the Psalmist says: “And He gave them favor before those who took them captive” (Ps 106:46). As God hardened the heart of Pharaoh to be glorified in the salvation of His people, He gave kindness in the heart of the prince of the eunuchs that God might be glorified in Daniel and his companions. Thus He gives us assurance that we may work for the sake of the One who moves the hearts of those around us, whether by permitting them to practice their violence or by changing it to kindness, so that all things work for our good.

1.4.4.en: * He who was taken captive because of the sins of his ancestors enjoyed an immediate reward for the greatness of his virtues. For he purposed in his heart not to be defiled with food from the king’s table, and preferred humble food to delicacies; therefore the Lord granted him a generous gift, for he received favor and tender love in the eyes of the prince of the eunuchs. By this we can understand that even in harsh circumstances the saints are loved by unbelievers, and this is by way of God’s mercies and not because of the goodness of the corrupt.

1.4.5.en: St. Jerome. “And the prince of the eunuchs said unto Daniel:

1.4.6.en: I fear my lord the king, who hath appointed your meat and your drink:

1.4.7.en: for why should he see your faces worse liking than the children which are of your sort? then shall ye make me endanger my head to the king.”

1.4.8.en: Then said Daniel to the chief of the cupbearers, whom the prince of the eunuchs had set over Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah:

1.4.9.en: Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink.

1.4.10.en: Then let our countenances be looked upon before thee, and the countenance of the children that eat of the portion of the king’s meat: and as thou seest, deal with thy servants.

1.5.0.en: So he consented to them in this matter, and proved them ten days” [10-14].

1.5.1.en: The young Daniel was living in a foreign land (the land of captivity), and he could have made excuses for not fasting. Daniel was in an environment that encouraged sin, because he was in the king’s palace. And he was obliged to eat every day of the king’s delicacies and the wine which he drank.

1.5.2.en: He practiced fasting even in his old age (Dan 10), as though Daniel’s heart never grew old.

1.6.s.en: What is observed in the fast of the prophet Daniel:

1.6.0.en: A. The prophet Daniel practiced his fast not merely by abstaining from food, but it is said: “He purposed in his heart” [8]. For the spiritual life is the enjoyment of an inner treasure. “Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Mt 6:21). Thus the sincere spiritual life begins from the depths of the heart, so that when the hour of temptation comes, the believer, by the divine grace working in him, can resist and overcome, bearing the power of the holy will within him. On the other hand, the matter did not stop at the limits of the heart, but he turned what was in his heart into action. For worship begins in the depths but is also translated into practice, so the body shares with the soul, and work with thought, and man practices his spiritual life with his whole being, hidden and visible.

1.6.1.en: B. He asked the prince of the eunuchs not to be defiled. This request was reckoned among the impossibilities for the prince of the eunuchs, because its cost was his neck, without any discussion.

1.6.2.en: Daniel believed that God, the God of the impossible, would work in the heart of this pagan man, as long as the matter concerned the holiness and purity of his life. The prince of the eunuchs had changed their names, but he was unable to change their hearts and their holy nature in the Lord.

1.7.s.en: Daniel counted the king’s delicacies as defilement. Why?

1.7.0.en: · Because his brethren were deprived of the luxurious life, so how could he live in the palace in a life of luxury while others were in need?

1.7.1.en: · Because what was set on the table might contain foods forbidden according to the Mosaic law, such as what is strangled and the flesh of certain forbidden animals, those that do not part the hoof and do not chew the cud. Though without doubt many kinds of meats were served at the king’s table, and Daniel and his companions could choose the permitted meats.

1.7.2.en: · These captive young men feared that the king’s delicacies would distract them from knowing their true position as captives. They do not seek the king’s table but their own freedom and that of their people. Their hearts would not settle in a foreign palace; rather they longed to return to their homeland. Without doubt Daniel and his companions were groaning within themselves for what had befallen the people, the temple and the holy city, so they wanted to remain in a state of inner bitterness until God would have compassion on them and bring back the captivity.

1.7.3.en: · Daniel feared those who share at the table as addicts of wine, so he refused wine entirely, and it is said: “For those who are addicted to wine, who go in to seek mixed drink: do not look at the wine when it is red, when it shows its bubbles in the cup and goes down smoothly” (Prov 23:30-31). Perhaps Daniel counted himself a Nazirite to the Lord who drinks neither wine nor strong drink (Num 6:2-3). The priests were forbidden to use it before the service of the temple (Lev 10:1-9), and kings were forbidden to use it (Prov 31:4-5). And as we saw before, these youths were in inner bitterness because of the captivity, so how could they drink wine, the sign of joy? They abstained from it until God would bring back their captivity.

1.7.4.en: St. Hippolytus of Rome says: [Blessed are those who keep the covenant of their fathers and do not disobey the law given by Moses, but fear God who was revealed through him. These, though captives in a strange land, were not lured by the savory meats, nor did they become slaves to the pleasures of wine, nor did the enticement of the glory of princes seize them; but they kept their mouths holy and pure, and with these mouths they praised the heavenly Father.]

1.7.5.en: * He who did not wish to eat or drink from the king’s table and wine lest he be defiled (especially if he knew that the wisdom and teaching of the Babylonians were false) would not agree to utter what is false.

1.7.6.en: St. Jerome. Daniel entered into a dialogue marked by courage and boldness, with confidence and gentleness and in a spirit of humility, not self-righteousness. It is as though true religious life is the practice of moderation, so that man neither lives cringing in humiliation, nor yet violent and disrespectful of others, nor haughty as one who is more righteous than they.

1.7.7.en: Daniel was marked in his dialogue by wisdom and dignity, with the faith that the One who moves his heart and the heart of others is God. It is as though we must put a hidden element into the dialogue, namely “God’s intervention for our spiritual good.” It is clear from [9] that the fruit of the dialogue and its results were not the doing of Daniel’s personality alone, but a grace that God offered him by His mercies in the eyes of the prince of the eunuchs. For the hearts of those in authority over us, even if they are unbelievers or harsh, are in the hand of God, who moves them for our sake. “The king’s heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will” (Prov 21:1).

1.7.8.en: God Himself wants us to converse with Him, as Abraham, Moses, David and others entered into a dialogue with Him.

1.7.9.en: C. Daniel and his friends fasted ten days in earnest and labored, and God gave them tenfold. He gave them a good appearance and they became fatter than all the youths. What happened with them was not natural but a gift from God. Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God (Deut 8:3).

1.7.10.en: * They knew that it is not earthly flesh that gives men beauty and strength, but the grace of God which the Word bestows.

1.7.11.en: St. Hippolytus of Rome. He gave them knowledge, understanding and wisdom, for moderate spiritual fasting does not weaken the mind but supports it, establishes it and makes it grow.

1.8.0.en: D. This book presents to us a living picture of the fast of Daniel, who was content with vegetables (pulse [12]), abstaining from eating meat (Dan 10:3) as he abstained from every luxury, from drinking wine and from anointing with oil (Dan 10:3). The Psalmist practiced fasting in the same way, for he says: “My knees trembled from fasting, and my flesh became lean from eating oils” (Ps 109:24). Fasting from food is also accompanied by repentance and remorse (Dan 10:2).

1.8.1.en: * His faith was exceedingly great, for he not only promised that he would be in bodily health by eating the humble food, but also fixed a time for it. This was not rashness on his part but a matter of faith. By this faith he despised the king’s sumptuous food.

1.9.0.en: “15 And at the end of ten days their countenances appeared fairer and fatter in flesh than all the children which did eat the portion of the king’s meat. 16 Thus the chief of the cupbearers took away the portion of their meat, and the wine that they should drink; and gave them pulse” [15-16].

1.9.1.en: We do not know the number of the young men who were chosen to serve the king and assist him in his work. Without doubt they were many, but we know by name only Daniel and his three friends. Since they were earnest in their faithfulness to God in everything despite the harsh circumstances, and submissive to His will whatever it cost them, they deserved to have their names recorded in the Holy Bible and engraved in the book of eternal life.

1.10.s.en: 5. Their enjoyment of wisdom and understanding:

1.10.0.en: “As for these four children, God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams” [17].

1.10.1.en: God fulfilled His promise to His believers: “Them that honour me I will honour” (1 Sam 2:30).

1.10.2.en: * Note that it is said that God gave the holy youths knowledge and learning in secular literature, in every book or branch of wisdom.

1.10.3.en: St. Jerome. God distinguished Daniel not only from the rest of the people but even from his holy companions, to prepare him for the accomplishment of an important prophetic work. St. Jerome sees that God gave the four youths wisdom and knowledge, but added to Daniel the understanding of visions and dreams, so that what others see in appearance as a shadow he could perceive clearly with the eyes of understanding. Thus God gave the four youths knowledge and understanding with wisdom in Chaldean literature and conduct, but Daniel was distinguished from his companions by the spirit of prophecy, for God gave him understanding of visions and dreams, to reveal the will of God and His plan. God forbade the use of magic under the pretext of knowing the future (Deut 18:10), but He does not withhold from His prophets the disclosure of some aspects of the future for the edification of His people and the glory of His holy name.

1.11.s.en: 6. Their superiority over all the magicians:

1.11.0.en: 18 Now at the end of the days that the king had said he should bring them in, then the prince of the eunuchs brought them in before Nebuchadnezzar. 19 And the king communed with them; and among them all was found none like Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah: therefore stood they before the king. 20 And in all matters of wisdom and understanding, that the king enquired of them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and astrologers that were in all his realm. 21 And Daniel continued even unto the first year of king Cyrus.

1.11.1.en: “Now at the end of the days that the king had said he should bring them in, then the prince of the eunuchs brought them in before Nebuchadnezzar.

1.11.2.en: And the king communed with them; and among them all was found none like Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah:

1.11.3.en: therefore stood they before the king.

1.11.4.en: And in all matters of wisdom and understanding, that the king enquired of them, he found them ten times better than all the magicians and astrologers that were in all his realm” [18-20].

1.11.5.en: The king could not have tested these young men had he not himself been wise, knowledgeable and of high culture. The king was pleased with them because he did not bring them to the palace for amusement with vain tales and talk or pleasant jesting, but to assist him in a spirit of wisdom and seriousness.

1.11.6.en: God was glorified in His captive servants, for they surpassed all their Chaldean colleagues who boasted that they were possessors of wisdom by birth, counting others barbarians and ignorant. Now their king acknowledges that their wisdom is nothing before the abundance of God’s grace.

1.12.0.en: “And Daniel continued even unto the first year of king Cyrus” [21].

1.12.1.en: This does not mean that Daniel remained only until the first year of King Cyrus, but he wanted here to affirm that Daniel lived through the period of the captivity until its end, for in this year the Jews returned to Jerusalem.

1.12.3.en: * Let the enemy carry me to the palace of Babylon, but he cannot bring my soul down from heaven!

1.12.4.en: Let him offer me all the delicacies and pleasures, but he will not tear me away from the heavenly table!

1.12.5.en: Rather I shall enjoy the bread of angels!

1.12.6.en: * Grant me to fast from the love of the world, and You will grant me blessing for my body, my soul and my mind.

1.12.7.en: You will support me with Your heavenly wisdom, and reveal to me Your surpassing mysteries!

1.12.8.en: * As You were with Daniel in the palace of his exile, accompany me by Your grace wherever I may be!

1.12.9.en: You will grant me success in every work to which my hands reach out!
